_README: Hand rulings on individual facts, keyed by SCIENTIFIC name. Read after the model and after the refute pass, immediately before emit, so a ruling survives every re-bake. null (or {"fact": null}) suppresses the fact; a string replaces it and marks it as hand-written. Use this for claims that are widely repeated and still wrong — the refute pass only catches what is checkably false, not what is merely universal.

Heterodontus portusjacksoni.fact: Females lay a spiral-flanged egg case and wedge it into a rock crevice, where the surge cannot pull it free.
Heterodontus portusjacksoni.why: Replaces the model's line, which had her carrying the case in her mouth "to screw them in tighter". The spiral flange is a feature of the case, not evidence of a screwing action, and the refute pass passed the claim because every popular source repeats it. The wedging is real, so the fact is corrected rather than dropped. Marco, 4 Sep 2026.

Achoerodus viridis.fact: Every blue one is a male, and every male started out as a female — the change comes late in a long life, and a brown fish alongside may be either. They can pass 35 years, and they spend a good deal of it eating sea urchins, cracked with peg teeth and crushing plates in the throat.
Achoerodus viridis.why: The model's line was refuted, correctly, for saying that turning blue IS the sex change and that it is triggered by the resident male disappearing: blue-phase females occur, and no harem control is documented in A. viridis. But the refute pass is all-or-nothing, so the true half went with the false half and the bay's most-recorded fish ended up with nothing at all. This keeps what is supported — protogyny, 35-plus years, urchin predation — and drops the mechanism. Marco pointed out the gap, 6 Sep 2026.

Mola alexandrini.fact: The heaviest bony fish ever weighed was one of these — 2,744 kg, found off the Azores. It has no tail: the blunt rear edge is a fused plate built from the ends of the dorsal and anal fin rays, so it sculls with those two tall fins and looks like it is flying rather than swimming.
Mola alexandrini.why: Written by hand because this species was added in a session with no API key, so neither the fact pass nor the refute pass could run — the card says so rather than presenting it with the same warrant as a refuted-and-survived one. Both claims are specific to alexandrini rather than to sunfish generally: the weight record is often credited to Mola mola and belongs to this species, and the clavus is the thing you are looking at in the photograph. Marco asked for it, 6 Sep 2026. Worth re-running through the refuter on the next keyed bake.
